newsitem.title: UK: UK shares end weaker, dragged lower by weaker Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: UK shares end weaker, dragged lower by weaker Wall Street.

text.p: British shares greeted the long-awaited announcement of the country's election date with little excitement on Monday, looking instead to Wall Street for direction and closing lower as the Dow tumbled.

Prime Minister John Major ended months of speculation by setting Britain's election date for May 1. But the news failed to set pulses racing in the stock market -- analysts said the election date, and an expected victory for the opposition Labour Party, were already discounted.
The FTSE 100 index ended near the day's lows at 4,373.3, down 51.0. Ex-dividends accounted for 22.2 points of the fall.
Joe Rooney, strategist at Lehman Brothers, said the election announcement had little impact on the market.

"This can hardly come as a surprise, it was the date everyone was pencilling in and I don't think it will change perceptions towards the UK equity market," he said. "Markets are supposed to be rational discounters and there had been plenty of time to digest this."

The FTSE focused instead on Wall Street's weakness, falling as interest rate concerns rattled the U.S. market. The Dow was 55 points off as London closed and dealers said it would remain volatile ahead of March 25, when U.S. rates may be raised.

"Concerns on the U.S. interest rate front are beginning to tell," said David McBain, UK equity strategist at NatWest. "Clearly an increased risk of a pre-emptive move in interest rates is being factored in to share prices."
Dealers said U.S. CPI data on Wednesday and a triple-witching on Friday would keep the Dow volatile this week.

But McBain said that although the election announcement had little immediate impact, the market would now be focusing more closely on domestic political developments. "The UK market will keep a beady eye on events unfolding in the U.S. and that will undoubtedly go some way in setting the tone," he said.
"But while we knew the election was coming, now that we have a definite date set in stone, market participants will become much more closely focused on the political issues at hand."

The Labour Party is well ahead in opinion polls and is widely expected to form the next government. But although a Labour victory has been widely discounted, speculation about the size of its majority could still keep the market on its toes ahead of the election, analysts said.
If opinion polls were to indicate that Labour's lead was slipping, worries about a hung parliament with no single party in overall control could unsettle the FTSE.

"There is clearly an expectation that the outcome will be a Labour majority but if there is a worse scenario it could be that the polls get close near the election," said Ian Williams, strategist at Panmure Gordon.

Markets have traditionally regarded Labour with suspicion, but the party's recent attempts to move towards the centre ground in politics have prompted some analysts to view a Labour government with less trepidation.
"Ultimately we believe an incoming Labour government, which we must assume to be the most likely outcome, won't squander the reasonably robust economy they have inherited," McBain said.
"The election will provide short-term excitement but the longer term trend in the market is dictated by the strength of the economy, and that augurs well for the second half," he said.
Lonrho Plc shares were among the day's weakest, dropping 12p to 145-1/2, after a profits warning.
Cable and Wireless Plc shares climbed 5-1/2p to 511-1/2, boosted by reports that Deutsche Telekom AG was negotiating to buy a 14 percent stake.
Pearson Plc shares ended 14p weaker at 760 in the wake of the media and leisure group's annual results.
